title: Proofpoint model cascade & quantization playtest
body:
Purpose:
Short playtest notes for the Proofpoint POC: evaluate a two-stage cascade (small fast model -> larger fallback) with mixed quantization strategies and prompt orchestration to meet a 200ms p50 and <600ms p95 SLO while keeping hosted token cost below $3.50 per 1k output tokens for the classification+rewrite pipeline.

Background/context:
- Customer: Proofpoint (security SaaS). Throughput target: 30 qps sustained for planned pilot, spiky up to 180 qps.
- Workload: short-to-mid prompts (input size 40-400 tokens), outputs 20-180 tokens. Typical patterns: high volume automated classification, plus occasional more complex rewrite/summarization for escalations.
- Constraints: data residency ok for hosted, but must support optional private deployment. Latency + cost are primary decision drivers.

Objectives for this playtest:
1) Establish a cascade architecture that keeps ~80% requests on small model while maintaining >=95% accuracy vs baseline for classification and >=90% quality for rewrites.
2) Measure latency and cost delta for quantization strategies: 8-bit PTQ, 4-bit QAT-proxy (simulated), and mixed FP16/4-bit per layer.
3) Exercise prompt orchestration: prefix caching, short-circuiting for deterministic prompts, and confidence-based fallback routing.

Model candidates evaluated (notes):
- tiny-encoder (E3-small-decoder-compat) 3.2B encoder-decoder, fast for classification, supports chunked encoder runs; strong for short inputs, better token-efficiency for classification but weaker on open-ended rewrite.
- mid-decoder (D7.5) 7.5B decoder-only, strong all-rounder, good latency/quality balance.
- large-refine (D13) 13B decoder with refinement loop (two-pass), used only as final fallback for low-confidence or high-recall cases.

Tradeoffs observed:
- Encoder-decoder models have cheaper encoder cost for short inputs but require merge step; observed ~10% higher p95 due to merge overhead on low-batch scenarios.
- Decoder-only mid model consistently outperformed tiny encoder on rewrite diversity at comparable latency when quantized to 8-bit.

Quantization strategies tried:
- PTQ-8 (symmetric, per-channel): straightforward, stable, small quality drop (~1.5% accuracy on classification).
- PTQ-4 (GPTQ-like): aggressive, significant size drop, larger quality variance across prompt shapes; unstable on some attention patterns.
- QAT-proxy (fake quant during finetune-ish pass): simulated here by bias-correction post-processing and short fine-tune on 2k annotated examples; reduced 4-bit quality gap substantially.
- Hybrid (encoder FP16 + decoder 4-bit / or attention kernels in FP16): found to stabilize generation for encoder-decoder hybrid and preserve coherence for longer outputs.

Key experiments (matrix):
- Run A: tiny-encoder in PTQ-8, mid-decoder in PTQ-8 fallback -> baseline cascade.
  Results: 78% served by tiny-encoder; p50 120ms, p95 540ms, classification acc 94.6% (baseline 95.8%).
- Run B: tiny-encoder PTQ-8, mid-decoder PTQ-4 fallback -> faster tail but mid-decoder quality dropped on few-shot rewrites. p95 450ms but rewrite BLEU-like eval -5 pts.
- Run C: tiny-encoder FP16 + mid-decoder hybrid(4-bit decoder + FP16 attention) -> best quality/latency balance. p50 130ms, p95 410ms, cost per 1k output tokens estimated $2.8.
- Run D: mid-decoder primary (no encoder cascade), PTQ-4 with QAT-proxy corrections -> served 100% at mid latency, quality close to hybrid but cost up ~18%.

Routing and fallback heuristics implemented/tested:
- Confidence metric: logit-gap (top1-top2 normalized) computed from decoder logits for final token; threshold tuned to retain precision.
- Latency budget routing: if small-model latency predicted > SLO (e.g., queued), route to mid-decoder directly to reduce tail.
- Cost cap routing: route high-cost customers to small-model-only profile; support per-customer routing config.
- Deterministic short-circuit: for deterministic classification prompts (pattern match + high token overlap with cached prefix), short-circuit to cached result. Observed cache hit rate ~22% for classification traffic after 48h warmup.

Prompt/pipeline orchestration notes:
- Prompt templates: kept minimal variable context; moved long context to retrieval step with embeddings and token-windowing; prefix caching applied to top-3 retrieval results.
- Few-shot vs instruction: for classification, single instruction + 2 examples performed better in small model than 6-shot; fewer shots reduce token cost and improve latency.
- Post-processing: implemented lightweight reranker (logit-based and embedding-similarity) inside mid-decoder fallback stage to filter hallucinations.

Operational metrics (sample):
- Target SLO: p50 <200ms, p95 <600ms for mixed workload.
- Run C achieved p95 410ms (meets SLO).
- Average unit cost: Run C ~$2.8 / 1k output tokens; Run A ~$3.2; Run B ~$2.4 but worse quality.
- Model memory footprints (quantized): tiny-encoder PTQ-8 ~12GB, mid-decoder hybrid ~22GB, mid-decoder PTQ-4 ~10GB.

Observations and gotchas:
- 4-bit PTQ unstable for certain prompt templates that exercise rotary/continuous position embeddings — observed decoding stalls in ~0.6% of samples; QAT-proxy mitigated but required labeled examples covering edge cases.
- Prefix caching effective but requires cache TTL tuning. Must invalidate cache when prompt template changes or when model variant changes (quantization swap).
- KV cache across mixed-precision backends tricky: when routing between models, don't reuse raw KV objects; instead reuse embeddings or chunked prefix output to reconstruct.
- Metrics plumbing: need token-level cost attribution per route/model in Redwood Console for accurate chargeback; current console setup required a small instrumentation PR (linked above).

Acceptance testing (customer-facing):
- Create 250-case eval set from Proofpoint logs (anonymized) split 80/20 for tuning/validation.
- Pass criteria: classification F1 >= baseline-0.03, rewrite human rating >= baseline-0.90 in blind eval of 200 samples.
- Stability pass: <0.5% stall/failure rate under 200qps sustained for 30m.

Runbook checklist for next steps before pilot handoff:
- [ ] Lock model-cascade config: tiny-encoder FP16 (encoder) + decoder 4-bit fallback hybrid.
- [ ] Implement routing guardrails: confidence thresholds, queued-latency routing.
- [ ] Add QAT-proxy fine-tune pass for 4-bit decoder on 2k labelled examples (sensitive to distribution).
- [ ] Instrument per-route token cost in console (PR #1123).
- [ ] Add cache invalidation hook on prompt-template deploy.
- [ ] Prepare customer docs: expected latency/cost tradeoffs, fallback behavior, SLA notes.

Open questions / risks:
- Is QAT-proxy allowed for customer's compliance posture? Need legal sign-off if model snapshots are trained on customer examples.
- For private deployment, can we ship hybrid quant kernels (4-bit + FP16 attention) across their on-prem GPUs (A100 vs H100 differences)? Need infra compatibility check.
- How does dynamic routing affect accountability for audit logs? Need to store routing-decisions per request for debugging.

Quick experiment ideas to run next:
- Per-layer sensitivity map for 4-bit quant: try keeping feedforward layer 1 in FP16 while quantizing others.
- Logit-gap calibration per prompt-type instead of global threshold.
- Micro-batching effect: test continuous batching with 8-20ms batching window to see cost vs latency inflection point.

Notes-to-self / meeting action items:
- Priya to run QAT-proxy job with 2k annotated examples (due 2025-10-09).
- Ethan to validate kernel compatibility on customer H100 in staging (due 2025-10-06).
- Luca to prepare short pilot runbook and one-pager for Proofpoint legal (due 2025-10-03).

Appendix: quick CLI snippets used in playtest:
- start tiny model (FP16 encoder + 8-bit decoder): redwoodctl deploy --model tiny-enc --quant encoder=fp16,decoder=8bit --pool small-32
- route rule example (pseudocode): if logit_gap < 0.08 or latency_estimate > 300ms => route to mid-decoder

End of playtest notes. This file is a working artifact — draft results for internal review before customer readout.
